The test image shows a soybean stem/root with:
- Dark brown to nearly black necrotic lesion on the upper portion
- Tan/yellow transition zone in the middle
- Healthy green tissue at the base
- Affected part: stem/root junction area

This pattern suggests a stem rot disease. Top candidates: Phytophthora (chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending upward), Rhizoctonia (reddish-brown sunken lesions at soil line), or Pythium damping off.

The Phytophthora reference shows wilted field plants but not the clear stem lesion pattern. 

Analyzing the test image more carefully: the image shows what appears to be a soybean seedling/plant held up, with:
- Very dark (black-brown) necrotic tissue at the upper stem/root junction area
- Fibrous dead root-like structures extending from the dark area
- A tan/yellowish transition zone below
- Healthy green stem at the base

This pattern of dark brown to black lesion at the soil line/hypocotyl area transitioning to tan then healthy green is characteristic of **Phytophthora** stem rot (chocolate-brown discoloration from below soil line extending upward) or **Rhizoctonia** (reddish-brown dry canker at soil line).

The darkness and sharp transition from necrotic to healthy tissue, combined with the stem location, is most consistent with Phytophthora — which causes the classic chocolate-brown to dark stem discoloration extending upward from the soil line.
